title: Evaluate signed netconsole capture for GB10 kernel output before silent freezes
failure: A DGX Spark Founders Edition (DGX OS, kernel 7.0.0-1019-nvidia, open driver 580.173.02, BIOS 5.36_0ACUM018) reportedly hard-froze with off-host 10-second telemetry still available up to the last sample but no Xid, NVRM, OOM, hung_task, panic, or pstore record. A different Spark owner reports netconsole loaded and emitted its start message with Secure Boot enabled using the signed build-time module; no real freeze was captured by it.
current_coverage: The optional UDP exporter sends selected telemetry fields; it does not send kernel printk. Local journal/pstore analysis cannot recover messages that never reached those sources.
gap_or_complement: Evaluate persistent signed netconsole to an operator-controlled receiver as an independent kernel-message path, with Secure Boot intact, timestamp/boot correlation and receiver-freshness reporting. This augments diagnosis; it does not recover the host or prove a cause when no printk is emitted.
evidence_level: medium: one detailed silent-freeze report plus another Spark owner's Secure Boot module-load confirmation; exact target-kernel persistence and incident capture remain untested.
risks: UDP netconsole is unencrypted and unacknowledged; kernel logs can expose host details.
The remote receiver or route can fail with the host's network path.
No message during a freeze cannot distinguish absent kernel output from failure of the logging path.
closure: With Secure Boot enabled on a named GB10 OEM/kernel/driver, prove module signature and receiver path, capture a kernel marker off-host, test no receiver/broken route controls, correlate boot identity/timestamps, and verify module/config removal. Mark real-freeze capture unverified absent an incident.

title: Validate RCU-stall panic and persistent capture as a GB10 recovery path
failure: On an ASUS/NVIDIA DGX Spark (BIOS GX10DGX.0103, Ubuntu 24.04, kernel 6.17.0-1008-nvidia, driver 580.142), the author reports an RCU-related hard freeze lasting 2h16m under mixed load, with 44 RCU stalls and an SBSA watchdog path that did not recover the lockup. kdump failed for the reported path. A manual panic test after enabling panic_on_rcu_stall and EFI pstore wrote pstore evidence; no later natural RCU incident demonstrated that the trigger recovered the host.
current_coverage: Adopted sysctl config declares hung_task_panic, softlockup_panic, hardlockup_panic and kernel.panic, but not panic_on_rcu_stall. FEATURE-KDUMP-PSTORE-PREAPAGADO checks kdump and reads dmesg captures; it explicitly leaves pstore support unverified.
gap_or_complement: Check whether RCU-stall panic can turn this specific kernel failure into reboot and preserve evidence through EFI pstore while keeping the existing kdump path valid. Treat forced-panic validation as proof of pstore arrival only, not recovery of a natural RCU stall or power interruption.
evidence_level: medium: one detailed owner report with exact OEM/kernel/driver and a manual panic-to-pstore test; causal mechanics for the failed kdump/watchdog path are partly hypothesized and no post-change natural RCU event is reported.
risks: A panic policy intentionally reboots the whole host and may lose unsaved work.
EFI pstore, kdump, crash-kernel, Secure Boot and watchdog behavior vary by OEM and kernel.
A CPU lockup may prevent the RCU panic path from executing; a power cut cannot be repaired by a software panic policy.
closure: On a canary GB10 stack, inventory active sysctl/boot/pstore/kdump state, test a controlled panic and verify pstore survives and bb scan reads it, preserve or justify changes to kdump, and prove rollback. Explicitly leave natural RCU-stall recovery unverified until an event or controlled RCU-specific fault injection exercises it.

title: Detect and recover Wi-Fi isolation without misclassifying a live host as frozen
failure: On one ASUS Ascent GX10 / GB10 with DGX OS 7.5.0, driver 580.173.02, kernel 6.17.0-1029-nvidia, and MediaTek MT7925/mt7925e, an AP band-steer roam was followed by a WPA timeout misreported as WRONG_KEY; NetworkManager entered failed/no-secrets and made no further reconnect attempt. The host remained locally healthy during a roughly 90-minute remote-access outage.
current_coverage: bb sample records traffic counters and gateway observations; bb scan analyzes rates; optional SSH probing targets loopback. No current record distinguishes a local host failure from a healthy host whose Wi-Fi association and management path failed.
gap_or_complement: Record local-versus-remote probe results, Wi-Fi association, supplicant authentication reason, NetworkManager state, and route freshness; define opt-in recovery for headless Wi-Fi. Test wired fallback and the reported BSSID/band-steering/autoconnect suggestions before recommending them as fixes. Other reports identify band selection and static DHCP as environment-specific workarounds; collect AP/SSID/security/adapter state and keep link association separate from DNS/mDNS management discovery.
evidence_level: medium: one detailed ASUS/MT7925 WPA-to-NetworkManager terminal-state report plus two separate network-path reports: arbitrary Wi-Fi disconnects reportedly mitigated by forcing 2.4 GHz (#356577), and campus PEAP/mDNS remote discovery reportedly solved by static DHCP (#350465). Those mitigations are owner reports without controlled A/B; they represent different causes and must not be conflated.
risks: A remote endpoint failure can be mistaken for local Wi-Fi failure unless local probes remain separate.
Automatic reconnection or connection changes can disrupt a valid link; opt-in configuration and verified rollback are required.
Evidence covers one OEM, adapter, driver, AP behavior, and software stack.
closure: Fixture the cited WPA timeout -> WRONG_KEY -> NetworkManager no-secrets transition while local probes remain healthy, plus a control host failure. Verify bb scan separates both and does not trigger a host reboot for network-only isolation. Run a bounded A/B roam/soak on the cited stack for each proposed recovery, report reconnect time and recurrence with literal commands/output, and verify rollback.

title: Validate lower GPU clock caps as an opt-in defense against silent power-offs
failure: Three forum reports describe GB10 power-offs/freezes with different stacks. The strongest evidence is thread 383624: three identical Founders Edition units, two with 14–15 days and zero stops, one with 14 stops in four days; 79,100 one-second samples showed temperature or low memory alone did not predict incidents, while hot+tight memory coincided with two of eight episodes, and four timestamped stops occurred during model load/unload. A 300,2100 cap lowered temperature in matched work and a 13-minute escalating test had zero failures. A separate HP ZGX Nano (580.178.04/kernel 7.0.0-1019) reports over 96h stable at 300,2200. Root cause remains unproven and the 13-minute test is not a sustained-stability demonstration. A separate DGX Spark owner (#364259) reports overheating and that `nvidia-smi -gtt 85` did not change it; NVIDIA states fan control is unavailable on Spark. The attached image was not inspected, and no stack/workload/temperature series is available, so this is a separate unverified thermal concern rather than proof that a lower GPU clock cap fixes it. A separate owner says CPU/GPU throttle settings disappeared after reboot/update and the crash returned; another user recommended `nvidia-smi -lgc 0,2000` and reports lower power under heavy prefill, without a controlled run. No OEM/driver/firmware or causal diagnosis is supplied, and no report confirms the setting persists. A two-node A/B report (#365325) shows a persistent idle vLLM process can hold one GB10 near 2.4 GHz/10–11 W with near-zero GPU utilization while an otherwise matched node downclocks; stopping vLLM immediately restores low clock/power only on the affected node. Multiple config changes/reboots did not fix it, and the thread has no root cause.
current_coverage: The adopted atom-clock-lock unit declares 300,2800 at boot; this review did not verify the live driver's effective range. Blackbox records GPU clocks, temperature, power and throttle state. No local A/B tests whether a lower cap prevents silent power loss.
gap_or_complement: Perform a matched OEM/driver-specific A/B and soak before recommending a lower cap; capture performance cost and rollback to the actual Blackbox range. Keep the lower cap opt-in and per OEM until the mechanism and repeatability are established. Include reboot/update persistence and read-back of the effective cap in the canary experiment; forum commands are anecdotes, not a validated default. Include idle-model-loaded vs stopped baselines and a test for unexpected sustained clocks/power with zero utilization; avoid masking this behavior by capping clocks before the idle power-state cause is identified.
evidence_level: medium: multiple owner reports, including a same-hardware three-unit control group and one 96-hour post-change run; the only stated escalated zero-failure test after capping lasted 13 minutes, no local A/B exists, and no causal mechanism is confirmed.
risks: Peak performance and inference latency may worsen.
A lower clock may not address an adapter, board power, or airflow fault.
-rgc restores the driver maximum rather than Blackbox's 300,2800 policy; rollback must account for the persistent clock-lock unit.
closure: Matched baseline/capped runs on a named GB10 OEM with sustained inference, model load/unload and idle control, exact soak/failure counts, throughput/latency and sensor coverage; use identical units as controls where possible. Confirm effective clocks and demonstrate restoration of the declared 300,2800 policy. Predeclare soak and repeat; short runs do not close the stability claim.

title: Detect NVMe and filesystem failure before the GB10 becomes unbootable
failure: A DGX Spark owner reports a read-only filesystem and failed boot; the 4 TB NVMe remained visible in BIOS but GRUB could not write sectors. Official recovery image v1.91.51-1 ran about 10 hours, then reported filesystem checksum errors and a read-only transition; the unit remained unbootable and support called it an RMA candidate. Exact NVMe model/firmware, OEM/BIOS, kernel, SMART/NVMe health and kernel logs are absent, so physical drive failure is not established. A separate backup discussion (#369758) confirms owner concern about full-device backups on ARM64 and contains unverified community advice to boot a live USB, clone to an external SSD with ddrescue, then replace the internal drive; the claimed bootability of that clone has not been tested. A second Spark owner (#371868) reports that support’s NVMe test failed and was advised to request RMA; the post’s diagnostic photos were not inspected, so this corroborates an NVMe/RMA path without adding device state or cause. In another Spark (#356091), support reviewed BIOS/NVMe/recovery screenshots and called the machine an RMA candidate; those screenshots were not inspectable in this pass, so no state or cause is inferred.
current_coverage: Repository search across BB tools, bin, README and SPEC found no explicit NVMe health/SMART, kernel media-error threshold, or read-only filesystem transition monitor. Generic journal/evidence collection may preserve messages that exist, but no pre-failure disk-health signal is documented.
gap_or_complement: Evaluate a read-only monitor that records NVMe identity/firmware and available health/media-error counters, kernel I/O errors, mount read-only transitions, boot/device status and timestamped last-known-good data. On alert, preserve logs and health data and direct the operator to verified backup/recovery/RMA steps before repeated recovery writes. Use OEM-supported interfaces; do not run destructive self-tests or remediation writes against suspect media. Evaluate an independently tested backup/restore path for this architecture as part of data-preservation closure; treat the forum ddrescue/replacement suggestion as unvalidated until OEM boot/recovery behavior is proven.
evidence_level: medium-low: one detailed owner report with failure sequence and support RMA guidance, but no logs or NVMe diagnostic output. The report is consistent with storage failure, not proof of its cause.
risks: Health counters may be unavailable or differ by NVMe OEM and firmware.
Repeated SMART tests or recovery writes could add load or destroy evidence on failing media.
A read-only state can originate above the physical device; alerts must not label the SSD defective without corroboration.
closure: On a named recoverable Spark/OEM stack, fixture NVMe media errors, filesystem remount-read-only, unavailable SMART permission/device and a healthy control. Verify BB records identity, values, event time, missing-data status and last-known-good samples without writing to the device; then rehearse backup/RMA evidence export and document recovery rollback. A live device-specific diagnosis remains unverified until matched to the reported OEM/firmware.

title: Separate desktop-session failures from a healthy remote GB10 host after updates
failure: A DGX Spark Founders Edition owner reports that after a Dashboard update one of two units repeatedly returns to the local login screen, while SSH and NVIDIA Sync remain functional. Reinstalling the desktop and applying another update did not fix the reported unit. NVIDIA requested a bug report; no report/result or exact package/kernel/OEM stack is present. A second user reports a similar login/credential symptom and changing a password helped that separate case, but cause and similarity are unverified. Related display reports include a Spark losing its display after the OS handoff and recovering after the owner disabled Wayland/restarted GDM (#356359), plus a black screen after overnight HDMI-switch use while SSH remained alive (#357519), reportedly improved by disabling screen blanking/lock. These owner-reported workarounds are not controlled, the latter reduces security, and neither proves a host freeze.
current_coverage: BB health/readiness uses host and service/network signals, including an optional loopback SSH banner probe. No explicit graphical login/session probe was found in the checked BB tools/docs; a healthy SSH path does not prove the local desktop login works.
gap_or_complement: Evaluate a low-impact desktop-session usability signal that records display-manager state, active user session and last login failure while keeping SSH/local host health separate. Preserve exact update package versions and journal evidence. A failed greeter must not trigger automatic host reboot or desktop package reinstall; collect state and offer a recoverable operator action first. Keep monitor/GDM/Wayland/blanking state separate from host/SSH health; capture a black-display incident without turning off security controls or restarting GDM automatically.
evidence_level: medium-low: one detailed post-update login-loop report with surviving SSH and failed reinstall attempts, plus one less-specific reply. No logs, exact update versions, or confirmed root cause.
risks: A headless system may intentionally have no graphical session, so absence alone cannot mean failure.
Restarting a display manager may terminate active desktop work or erase useful diagnostic context.
The reported password workaround came from another user and was not verified for the original case.
closure: Use fixtures for an intentionally headless system, a healthy desktop with working SSH, a greeter/login loop with healthy SSH, and a host-wide failure. Confirm the classification preserves the distinction and keeps all failed data collection as could_not_run. On a named recoverable Spark stack, capture a genuine post-update desktop session failure and verify no automatic reboot or package mutation occurs before a documented operator-approved recovery and rollback.

title: Detect a GB10 GPU that remains on PCIe but fails GSP initialization after boot
failure: After a subsequent boot, one Spark owner reports that `nvidia-smi` could not find the GB10 although PCI enumerated device `000f:01:00.0`, modules and `/dev/nvidia*` existed. CUDA initialization returned error 999 and the kernel logged repeated `RmInitAdapter: Cannot initialize GSP firmware RM`, `SEC2 secure boot partition timed out`, and `NV_ERR_TIMEOUT`. Field Diagnostics passed the previous day; NVIDIA requested a bug report and a second diagnostic run in the failed state. No report or exact stack was posted.
current_coverage: BB has GPU utilization/telemetry paths, but no explicit evidence in the cited forum of handling the split state “PCI device present, nodes/modules exist, GSP initialization failed and nvidia-smi has no devices.” A previous passing field diagnostic did not predict the next-boot state.
gap_or_complement: Evaluate an explicit GPU-ready probe that records NVML/nvidia-smi device enumeration and distinguishes PCI presence from usable CUDA/GSP state. Preserve the GSP/SEC2 kernel messages, boot identity, kernel/driver/GSP versions, Secure Boot state and field-diagnostic output when the probe fails. Report `GPU_UNAVAILABLE` and collection failures separately; do not auto-reload modules or power-cycle before capturing the failed-state evidence.
evidence_level: medium: one detailed symptom with exact device path and kernel messages; failed-state bug report/diagnostic and full software versions are missing, so root cause is undetermined.
risks: A GSP timeout may be transient or stack-specific; blanket module reloads can destroy evidence or worsen recovery.
nvidia-smi output and NVML availability differ with driver versions and permissions; probe must distinguish no GPU from command failure.
A prior field diagnostic passing does not establish device health after reboot.
closure: Build fixtures for healthy GPU, PCI visible but NVML/GSP unavailable, PCI missing, Secure Boot/module rejection, and permission/command failure. Verify BB preserves raw messages and versions, reports GPU unavailability without calling it a whole-host freeze, and never resets the host automatically. On a named Spark/OEM stack, validate against a naturally failed state or a vendor-approved fault injection and rerun Field Diagnostics before/after without erasing evidence.

title: Verify SBSA watchdog availability before interpreting repeated GB10 reboots
failure: A Spark owner reports repeated crashes/reboots every few minutes despite trying kernels 6.14 and 6.17 and current firmware; Field Diagnostics crashed at varying points. Another poster suggested checking `lsmod | grep sbsa_gwdt`; the owner confirmed the module was not running and said the machine was stable “for now”, but did not state an action or duration. A separate answer reports `wdctl` showing an SBSA watchdog with a 10-second timeout and another participant suggested disabling watchdog during debugging. Causation is unproven.
current_coverage: BB already uses systemd/hardware watchdog recovery and separates watchdog from panic/pstore observations; repository search found no explicit boot-time check recording SBSA watchdog device/module availability together with BIOS watchdog enablement. Absence from `lsmod` alone may be valid if driver is built-in.
gap_or_complement: Evaluate a read-only boot health record for watchdog capability and ownership: `/dev/watchdog*`, `/sys/class/watchdog`, systemd watchdog logs/status, kernel built-in/module state, BIOS setting if exposed, and `wdctl` timeout. On repeated resets, correlate boot ID and pstore before changing watchdog policy. Never treat disabling the watchdog as a production fix; preserve current policy and require OEM support before changing it.
evidence_level: low-medium: repeated failures and a reported absent module are described, but the author never states what action preceded stability, no exact OEM/BIOS/driver is supplied, and no pstore/diagnostic output is included.
risks: A missing `lsmod` entry may indicate built-in driver rather than missing support.
Disabling the hardware watchdog can turn recoverable lockups into permanent outages and remove evidence of reset cause.
Watchdog ownership and firmware controls differ across OEMs and kernel builds.
closure: On a named, recoverable Spark stack, fixture loaded-module, built-in driver, no device, BIOS-disabled, permission-denied and healthy states; prove read-only detection and no policy mutation. For an actual repeated-reset case, correlate exact boot/BIOS/kernel/driver, `/sys/class/watchdog`, `wdctl`, journal and pstore before/after; reproduce only with OEM-approved fault injection and verify rollback. Do not claim that module absence caused a reboot from this forum report alone.

title: Make GB10 unified-memory profiling blind spots explicit and evaluate a supported alternative
failure: A GB10/SM121 owner using driver 580.95.05, CUDA 13.1 and Nsight Systems 2026.1.1 cannot trace UVM CPU/GPU page faults or migrations; explicit tracing flags produce the same unsupported message. NVIDIA confirms UVM profiling is unsupported on Spark and says it is being worked on.
current_coverage: Blackbox captures host memory pressure and GPU-level signals, but the forum confirms Nsight Systems cannot provide UVM attribution on this platform/stack. Aggregate counters cannot prove a specific GPU page migration or fault caused an incident.
gap_or_complement: Record whether the exact GB10 driver/tool combination supports UVM trace before relying on it. Evaluate a vendor-supported replacement when available; until then label UVM migration attribution unavailable rather than infer it from host counters.
evidence_level: high that UVM tracing is unsupported on the cited stack (NVIDIA forum response); low on availability/date of a future replacement.
risks: A capability probe can go stale with driver/tool releases.
Host page-fault totals are not GPU UVM trace and may misattribute activity.
Adding unsupported profiler flags can alter workload behavior.
closure: On the named GB10 driver/tool versions, reproduce the unsupported response, ensure Blackbox records the capability gap once with versions, then test the first vendor-supported replacement against an ordinary host-memory control and known UVM workload. Do not mark page migration attribution available until traces are verified.

title: Prove ConnectX-7 data-plane recovery after link re-enumeration
failure: A four-node GB10 cluster reports NCCL all_gather falling 192→25 Gbps after a live cable replug while mlxlink still reports Active/200G; another node reports PCIe bridge retraining failure and missing NIC. Similar E-Switch removal is expected when no cable is attached, so these cases need separate states.
current_coverage: Existing CX7 hotplug card addresses hotplug behavior and service signals; link presence alone does not establish collective health. One Field Diagnostics run reportedly passed while CX7 was nonfunctional.
gap_or_complement: Track supported-cable presence, PCIe endpoint/retraining, mlx5 bind, firmware/BDF and representative NCCL throughput as separate readiness dimensions. Persist AER and power warnings with workload throughput. Treat missing interface as expected only when no supported cable is connected; require post-relink collective A/B before marking recovery.
evidence_level: medium-high for reported performance regression and false-green link state; low for root cause/cable qualification (one attached bug report unread).
risks: 27W PCIe warning also appears on a healthy 200G node and cannot identify cause alone.
Disabling hotplug can remove intended function and must be OEM-validated with rollback.
closure: On exact GB10/OEM/firmware/kernel/driver/cable/switch, repeat baseline and cable transition; show detector fails when NCCL degrades despite 200G link, passes after real recovery, and ignores expected no-cable E-Switch teardown. Preserve crash bundle/RMA path for retraining failure.

title: Block unapproved unattended ConnectX firmware writes
failure: One ASUS GX10 owner reports dpkg --configure triggering mlnx-fw-updater 25.10-1.7.1.0 from DOCA baseos8-latest, changing CX7 PSID NVD0000000087 from 28.45.4028 to 28.47.1088 despite a BME/DMA prerequisite warning; both devices then stayed in pre-init timeout -110 through OS reinstalls. NVIDIA says engineering had not reproduced. Separately, NVIDIA explicitly says driver 595 is unsupported on Spark after users report kernel/driver loss and failed boot during apt transitions.
current_coverage: APT critical package guard and kernel/initrd gate cover package graph and module presence; the reported DOCA firmware updater could flash firmware during generic package configuration, before users approve an OEM-specific update.
gap_or_complement: Fail closed on firmware writes invoked by general apt/dpkg/unattended upgrades. Allow only exact OEM/PSID/version/source combinations, enforce BME/DMA/driver readiness, block on any prerequisite warning, verify flash target and recovery bundle, and stage a tested fallback. Apply the same supported-version allowlist to driver series and require matching modules for next boot.
evidence_level: High that apt kernel/driver mismatch can remove nvidia.ko and NVIDIA stated 595 unsupported; low-to-medium for CX7 flash-to-brick causality until unread mstdump/nvidia-bug-report and engineering reproduction.
risks: A firmware guard that blocks valid signed OEM updates can delay security/reliability fixes.
Unofficial manual flash or package-purge recipes can strand device or void warranty.
closure: Simulate apt/dpkg transactions with unsupported driver and firmware package; verify no firmware write starts, target kernel has matching supported module, unsupported OEM/PSID/version and BME-not-ready cases fail closed, approved transaction writes exact signed image, and recovery/RMA evidence is retained.

title: Expose thermal and platform sensor blind spots by OEM
failure: ASUS GX10 user reports sustained inference with ACPI zones 0/5 at 96.6C, GPU thermal slowdown active and fan telemetry N/A; later posts contain distinct hard cutoffs, including one at reported 79C with power loss and OOM lines preceding some outages. Retail Spark audit reports DCGM energy fields cover GPU but no CPU/SoC/powercap energy; community sensor module is blocked by Secure Boot on retail. NVIDIA says FE did not reproduce the OEM case.
current_coverage: Thermal readiness tracks GPU temp/throttle and platform thermal signals; fan RPM/PWM and CPU/SoC energy channels may be unavailable and coverage differs by OEM/firmware.
gap_or_complement: Report per-source sensor capability, staleness and absent fan/rail coverage; capture synchronized GPU/ACPI/clock/counter/workload/journal/firmware versions. Keep thermal throttling, OOM, and abrupt power loss as distinct event classes; do not claim fan curve or firmware root cause from correlation. Use only stable signed OEM firmware unless vendor gives test channel procedure and rollback.
evidence_level: High for user-reported synchronized ASUS thermal telemetry; medium for cross-firmware relationship; low for causal fan/thermal diagnosis because attached archives were not inspected and NVIDIA could not reproduce on FE.
risks: No Linux fan PWM/RPM makes fan attribution inferential.
Cross-OEM capsule testing or downgrade can brick or void warranty.
Missing CPU energy data must not be presented as total system energy.
closure: On exact OEM SKU, run controlled inference soak with synchronized sensor coverage/clock/throttle/journal receipt, prove gaps are visible, compare stable vendor firmware only under approved A/B and rollback, test power-loss and OOM classifiers separately, and retain independent power-cut evidence.

title: Preserve official recovery path before updates or boot changes
failure: Forum user reports freeze after apt upgrade and a later Docker vLLM container with restart-always; after forced resets he could not reliably reach UEFI/recovery/SSH. NVIDIA recommended the official DGX recovery/reimage path, then seller/RMA when input/access recovery remained unavailable. Logs do not establish whether apt, workload, GRUB edits or another factor caused failure.
current_coverage: Rescue runbook covers no-boot, official reimage and RMA escalation; apt guard protects critical packages.
gap_or_complement: Before system upgrades or bootloader/driver changes, verify OEM-specific recovery media/UEFI entry and preserve user data. Track restart-on-boot workloads and put reversible admission bounds on resource-heavy services; after access loss follow vendor recovery rather than stacking unverified GRUB flags.
evidence_level: Medium for a severe recovery-path failure report; low for causal attribution and any suggested workload/memory fix.
risks: Reimage can destroy user data; confirm preservation before destructive recovery.
Unverified boot arguments may reduce recovery access or undermine Secure Boot.
closure: On each OEM model, rehearse official recovery media/UEFI access with data-preservation checkpoint, bounded rebooting workload, and documented support/RMA cutoff; simulate interrupted update without damaging production data.

title: Classify low GPU power only against a supported runtime baseline
failure: A thread initially reports GPU stuck at ~5W/0% under workload, then its author says the cause was old Driver 550.54.15/CUDA12.4; after GPU-burn installed Driver 580.95.05/CUDA13.0, GPU reached 96%/28W and power scaled normally. The mlx5 PCIe 27W message also appears on healthy idle Spark, so it is a false standalone indicator for GPU cap.
current_coverage: Runtime compatibility diagnostics capture active driver/CUDA stack; CX7 diagnostics capture PCIe slot power warning.
gap_or_complement: Before labeling platform power fault, record effective host/container driver+CUDA and run a known-good supported GPU load; keep mlx5 27W warning separate from GPU-side utilization/power/clock measurements.
evidence_level: Medium: forum author reports fix but diagnostic zip shared by DM was inaccessible.
risks: Initial setup was called stock before final post disclosed old driver/CUDA, showing provenance can be incomplete.
A single workload may fail for a model/kernel issue rather than power delivery.
closure: Reproduce on exact supported host/container stack; show healthy idle can emit mlx5 27W, stale runtime is rejected as unsupported, and supported GPU-burn plus inference correlate load/utilization/power correctly.

title: Test memory release and hard-failure evidence under long distributed inference
failure: Two posts report retained llama.cpp RPC memory reaching OOM and remote server memory requiring process kill/restart. Another ASUS GX10 author reports hard poweroff on long vLLM request while short torch/smoke passes; logs include failed CDI injection and later NV_ERR_NO_MEMORY, but no pstore and no evidence that memory caused the power loss.
current_coverage: Cgroup trace/soak and OOM attribution cover memory pressure; rescue/thermal receipts cover sudden unclean termination.
gap_or_complement: Add peer-attributed long-run/cross-node inference soak with RSS/PSS, cgroup events, UMA pressure, CDI state and GPU allocation errors, compare client disconnect/server stop for retained memory, and preserve last-good telemetry off-host before hard power loss. Do not automatically reboot or kill GPU workloads based on an OOM-like signal.
evidence_level: Medium for reported failures; low for true memory leak, memory causality, and poweroff mechanism.
risks: No exact runtime versions or per-process memory time series in these reports.
Hard power cut may be board/power/thermal failure, not OOM.
closure: On named model/backend/version, demonstrate baseline and sustained load, record process/cgroup/system counters, validate memory reclamation after server/client teardown, inject workload exhaustion in isolated test, and keep poweroff and OOM conclusions separate.

title: Fail closed before mounting external RAID below link-speed floor
failure: Owners report external USB NVMe enclosures renegotiating from 20Gbps to 480Mbps/~40MB/s, including after boot. An mdadm owner warns assembly at USB2 is unsafe after timeouts/resets and reports avoiding corruption by leaving the array unassembled/unmounted below 5000Mbps.
current_coverage: GX10 read-integrity probe covers checksums on file reads and internal NVMe/RAS evidence; it does not gate removable USB array assembly on current link speed.
gap_or_complement: Before mdadm assemble/mount, resolve member devices by stable identity, read effective per-device speed from sysfs, and keep all members unmounted if any fall below an OEM/operator-declared floor. Preserve state and require an explicit operator recovery action. Test UAS quirks only for exact VID/PID/enclosure with A/B; do not infer thermal cause from throughput alone.
evidence_level: Medium for observed USB renegotiation and safe-mount workaround; low for UAS/thermal/root-cause isolation (single owner reports, incomplete controlled A/B).
risks: Incorrect stable-device mapping or speed units can block healthy storage or mount the wrong device.
Disabling UAS can affect performance and device compatibility; kernel/module changes can impair boot.
External USB downgrade is not proof of internal GX10 NVMe corruption.
closure: On an isolated GB10 with named enclosure/drive/kernel/firmware, reproduce good and 480Mbps link states across cold boots, prove the array remains stopped and unmounted below threshold, prove it assembles after verified healthy negotiation, inject missing/stale sysfs readings and confirm fail-closed, measure boot/mount delay, and document config rollback.

title: Gate exact Ray/vLLM/Torch tensor-parallel stack and detect rank-progress stalls
failure: Two-Spark owner reports vLLM TP=2 lost one node after first prompt while peer GPU stayed at 100%; `--enforce-eager` changed symptom and owner later reported fixing their setup by using torch 2.9.1 instead of 2.10.0.
current_coverage: Runtime compatibility card captures supported versions; host hang capture does not necessarily distinguish dead distributed rank from GPU-busy/no-progress.
gap_or_complement: Track exact container digest/Torch/CUDA/vLLM/Ray/NCCL and TP/PP config. Validate known-good combinations; export per-rank request and collective progress/heartbeat alongside GPU busy/power. Bound request timeout and retain logs before process kill. Keep eager mode as A/B diagnostic only.
